addressed_problems.content: The study demonstrates that sparse and robust subnetworks (SRNets) exist in BERT-family models across three natural language understanding tasks (NLI, paraphrase identification, fact verification) under various pruning and fine-tuning paradigms. However, this investigation is limited to BERT-like encoders and these specific tasks; it remains unresolved whether SRNets with similar ID/OOD trade-offs exist across other model architectures such as encoder-decoder (e.g., T5) or autoregressive (e.g., GPT) PLMs, other task types including generation, dialogue, and multimodal understanding, and under other forms of dataset bias such as gender or racial biases in generation systems. Establishing the generality of the SRNet phenomenon would broaden the applicability of efficient and robust PLMs to a wider range of real-world scenarios.

The paper shows that mask training starting from intermediate checkpoints of BERT fine-tuning—for instance, after approximately 55% of the full fine-tuning steps—can produce SRNets comparable to those obtained after full fine-tuning, thereby reducing total training cost. However, the selection of the optimal checkpoint is determined empirically by observing training curves; an automatic method to predict the minimal fine-tuning point that yields near-optimal subnetwork performance without requiring full fine-tuning is not yet developed. Creating practical early-stopping or checkpoint-selection criteria that guarantee minimal computational cost while maintaining subnetwork ID and OOD performance remains an open problem, and its solution would make the SRNet search process more efficient and accessible.

The paper demonstrates that gradual sparsity increase from 70% to 90% combined with soft mask initialization improves the performance of SRNets at very high sparsity (e.g., 90%) compared to fixed sparsity training. Nevertheless, reliably identifying high-quality, low-variance SRNets at extreme sparsity levels still poses challenges, as performance drops and optimization instability persist. Further improvements in optimization stability and the ID/OOD trade-off in this regime are needed, and developing methods that consistently yield robust subnetworks at extreme parameter budgets remains an open direction.

The paper uses OOD training data (e.g., HANS, PAWS) during mask training to estimate an upper bound, revealing that almost unbiased BERT subnetworks exist within a standard fine-tuned BERT. However, whether comparable almost-unbiased subnetworks can be identified using only in-distribution data combined with bias models (e.g., product-of-experts, reweighting, or confidence regularization) without any OOD supervision is not resolved. Solving this open problem would eliminate the need for OOD data in the discovery of robust, unbiased subnetworks, making the approach more practical for real-world deployment where OOD examples are often unavailable or costly to obtain.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as BERT deliver strong in-distribution (ID) performance but face two intertwined, practically important scientific shortcomings that motivate this work. First, PLMs are large (e.g., BERT-base ≈ 110M parameters with ≈84M in Transformer layers), which imposes heavy memory and computational costs and prevents efficient deployment in resource-constrained settings; prior work has therefore pursued model compression (pruning, distillation, quantization, parameter sharing) and, more recently, the search for sparse subnetworks (lottery-ticket-style pruning and mask training) that preserve ID accuracy. Second, PLMs often rely on dataset biases (spurious correlations in training data) and thus generalize poorly to out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluations; prior debiasing approaches train models with bias-aware objectives (e.g., product-of-experts (PoE), example reweighting, confidence regularization) or construct OOD testbeds, but these efforts have focused on dense full models. Crucially, existing studies that find sparse PLM subnetworks demonstrating competitive ID performance have evaluated them only in ID regimes, leaving unresolved whether sparsification can be made compatible with robustness to dataset bias. As a result of these gaps, practitioners lack knowledge about whether sparse subnetworks can simultaneously (a) deliver substantially reduced parameter counts, (b) retain ID accuracy, and (c) improve or at least preserve OOD generalization under realistic debiasing objectives and across different pruning/fine-tuning paradigms (prune-after-finetune, prune-before-finetune with rewinding, or mask-training without parameter updates). The absence of systematic experiments combining compression methods, debiasing losses, and the three pruning/fine-tuning paradigms prevents quantitative assessment of this “sparsity versus robustness” trade-off, hinders principled choices for deployment, and leaves open whether one can find sparse, nearly unbiased subnetworks inside standard pre-trained or fine-tuned PLMs.

nodes.content: In applied NLU, practitioners require models that are both compact (to reduce inference cost and memory usage) and reliable on OOD data that breaks spurious correlations present in training sets. Prior compression research established that PLMs can be heavily pruned while retaining ID accuracy, but those findings were obtained almost exclusively under ID evaluation. Independently, debiasing research improved OOD performance for dense models but did not consider parameter-efficient alternatives. Without evidence that compression and robustness can coexist inside a single PLM instance, users cannot confidently trade parameter count for OOD robustness. This gap prevents deploying lightweight models with trustworthy OOD behavior and leaves unclear whether sparsification removes bias-related parameters or only discards nonessential capacity while leaving bias intact.

The standard lottery-ticket-style pipeline shows that sparse subnetworks can be rewound to early (often random or pre-trained) initializations and trained in isolation to recover ID performance. However, it was unknown whether such “trainable tickets” existing inside pre-trained BERT also encode solutions that are robust to dataset bias after downstream fine-tuning. If pre-trained tickets are biased in the same way as dense fine-tuned models, then fine-tuning them in isolation would not yield OOD robustness and would negate the practical benefits of compressing before task adaptation. Resolving whether pre-trained tickets can be both trainable and less biased is critical for producing compact, robust models without first fine-tuning and compressing a large dense model.

Two widely used approaches for finding sparse subnetworks are heuristic magnitude-based pruning (IMP) and explicit mask-optimization (mask training). Prior PLM compression studies used one or the other, but there was no systematic comparison in the OOD robustness setting. If the choice of pruning algorithm materially affects the ability to find SRNets, then practitioners need guidance on which method to use when robustness is a requirement. Without such comparison, one might choose a suboptimal pruning approach that either loses ID accuracy or fails to improve OOD generalization.

Standard pruning pipelines minimize the standard cross-entropy loss on ID data and therefore may preferentially remove parameters unrelated to ID loss while leaving bias-exploiting parameters intact. To obtain sparse models that are also robust, pruning procedures must take into account bias-aware objectives. Before this work, it was unclear whether integrating debiasing losses into the pruning stage would (a) be feasible, (b) produce better OOD generalization for the subnetwork, or (c) degrade ID accuracy. Demonstrating that debiasing-in-pruning yields SRNets clarifies how to combine compression with robustness-aware training objectives.

Evaluations that use only ID validation to select subnetworks cannot determine how unbiased a subnetwork could be if one had access to OOD signals. Practitioners therefore lack knowledge of the achievable robustness ceiling for a given PLM and sparsity budget. By explicitly using OOD data during mask training, one can empirically quantify an upper bound on how unbiased and robust a sparse subnetwork can become; prior to this work, no systematic empirical exploration of that upper bound for BERT existed across the three pruning/fine-tuning paradigms.

Searching for subnetworks by first fully fine-tuning the dense PLM and then performing mask training is computationally expensive. Alternatively starting from scratch (pre-trained weights) can be slower to converge and produce worse final results. There is therefore a need to identify practical checkpoints in the fine-tuning trajectory where mask training can be started to balance computational cost and subnetwork quality. Prior work did not provide actionable guidance on this timing in the OOD-robustness-aware setting, leaving practitioners to either over-train or accept suboptimal subnetworks.

At extreme sparsity levels (>70%), naively initializing mask training with the target sparsity sharply reduces optimization capacity and commonly causes optimization failure or severe performance drops. Practitioners need training strategies to find high-quality subnetworks under tight parameter budgets. Before this work, there was limited empirical guidance on how to adapt mask training schedules to preserve ID and OOD performance at very high sparsity.

The original LTH studies demonstrated trainable sparse subnetworks for ID tasks but did not consider robustness to dataset bias. It was unknown whether rewound subnetworks found in pre-trained BERT could be fine-tuned in isolation to produce robust models under debiasing losses. If LTH did not extend to OOD robustness, then compressing before fine-tuning would risk losing the ability to obtain robust task solutions; demonstrating this extension clarifies the feasibility of compress-then-adapt pipelines for robust deployment.

Observations made on a single PLM backbone might be idiosyncratic to that architecture or scale. To be useful, claims about SRNets must hold across model families and sizes. Prior work left unclear whether the coexistence of sparsity and bias-robust solutions is a quirk of BERT-base or a broader property of Transformer-based PLMs. Showing generalization to RoBERTa and BERT-large is necessary to support practical adoption across model choices.

Inside the BERT-base-uncased model there exist sparse subnetworks, obtained by applying a binary pruning mask to the Transformer-layer parameters (the 84 million parameters in the Transformer stack), that simultaneously (a) remove up to 70% of those Transformer-layer parameters and (b) preserve in-distribution (ID) performance while improving out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness. Concretely, across three natural language understanding tasks—natural language inference with MNLI as the ID set and HANS as the OOD set, paraphrase identification with QQP as the ID set and PAWS variants as the OOD sets, and fact verification with FEVER as the ID set and FEVER‑Symmetric as the OOD sets—and across three pruning/fine-tuning paradigms (1) pruning a fully fine-tuned BERT via iterative magnitude pruning that repeatedly zeros low-magnitude weights and retrains, (2) pruning the pre-trained BERT then fine-tuning the resulting subnetwork, and (3) mask training that learns binary masks over frozen weights via forward binarization and a straight‑through gradient estimator, subnetworks at sparsity levels up to 70% (i.e., retaining ≳30% of the 84M Transformer parameters) can (a) retain at least about 95% of the full dense BERT's ID metric (accuracy for MNLI/FEVER, weighted F1 for QQP) and (b) yield measurable OOD gains on HANS, PAWS, and FEVER‑Symmetric relative to the standard cross‑entropy (CE) fine‑tuned dense BERT.

metadata.narrative: The core experimental claim that sparse and robust subnetworks exist up to ≈70% sparsity is supported by broad empirical coverage across pruning paradigms and debiasing objectives (H1) and by OOD-supervised upper-bound experiments that show masks can reach very high OOD accuracy (H2). However, the claim is materially exposed to selection and statistical uncertainties: checkpoint selection is ID-driven in the main reported runs (P1), seed/sample variability is modestly constrained by only four runs and a small set of OOD benchmarks (P2), and mask-search success depends on tuned hyperparameters and schedules (P3). In effect, the paper gives good evidence that SRNets are achievable in the studied setups (credit from H1/H2), but the quantitative strength of the ID-retention (≳95%) and the magnitude of OOD gains are contingent on selection and hyperparameter choices (dominant risks: P1, P3); P2 amplifies the need for broader seed/dataset replication to raise confidence.

nodes.title: Sparse and robust subnetworks in BERT up to 70% sparsity retain ID and improve OOD

nodes.content: The pre-trained BERT-base-uncased contains subnetworks that can be identified before downstream fine‑tuning and then fine‑tuned in isolation to match or sometimes exceed the full dense model on both in‑distribution and out‑of‑distribution evaluations. Concretely, subnetworks found by (a) iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding (the train–prune–rewind pipeline that prunes during fine‑tuning and then rewinds subnetwork parameters to the pre‑training parameter vector θ_pt before isolated fine‑tuning) or (b) mask training applied to the pre‑trained weights (learning binary masks while keeping weights frozen and then fine‑tuning the masked model) and then fine‑tuned in isolation on the downstream task achieve comparable ID accuracy and improved OOD robustness at sparsity levels that depend on the task (typically up to roughly 50%–70% sparsity), thereby extending the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (the claim that sparse subnetworks exist that can be trained in isolation) to the setting where OOD robustness is evaluated.

metadata.narrative: There is credible empirical support that rewound pre-trained subnetworks can be fine-tuned in isolation to match or sometimes beat the dense model on ID and OOD in the authors' experiments (evidence in Fig. 4 and the LTH-style pipeline). The main risks are sensitivity to the rewind/pruning protocol and sparsity regime (P5) and the observed underperformance of some pre-trained-mask variants beyond ~50% sparsity (P6). Thus the extension of LTH to robustness is plausible within the studied budgets and rewind recipes, but its generality across sparsities and rewind choices remains limited until further sensitivity analysis removes P5/P6 as show-stoppers.

nodes.title: Pre-trained BERT contains rewound subnetworks fine-tunable in isolation to match or beat dense model

nodes.content: When searching for sparse and robust subnetworks in BERT-base-uncased, mask training—implemented by associating each frozen weight matrix with a real-valued mask, binarizing the mask in the forward pass, and updating the real-valued mask via straight‑through gradient estimation—generally yields better trade‑offs between ID performance and OOD robustness than iterative magnitude pruning (IMP), which repeatedly prunes smallest‑magnitude weights and retrains; this advantage of mask training is most consistent at moderate sparsity levels (e.g., up to 50%–70%), while IMP can be competitive only in some cases such as very high sparsity on certain tasks.

metadata.narrative: Comparative plots across tasks consistently show mask training outperforming IMP at moderate sparsity (H3), giving a substantive, actionable recommendation. The chief caveat is that this advantage depends on the specific mask/IMP implementations and hyperparameters (P7). Still, because mask-training wins across multiple tasks and pruning setups, the comparative strength is credible for the studied regime; further tuning of IMP could narrow the gap but would not negate the observed pattern without new evidence.

nodes.title: Mask training tends to find better SRNets than IMP at moderate sparsity

nodes.content: Incorporating debiasing objectives into the pruning or mask‑training stage increases the OOD performance of the resulting sparse subnetworks while largely preserving ID performance up to about 70% sparsity. In these experiments the bias degree β for each training example is computed from a separately trained bias model (the bias model takes hand‑crafted spurious features—e.g., word‑overlap features for MNLI/QQP and max‑pooled claim embeddings for FEVER—and outputs a class probability vector p_b, with β defined as the probability assigned to the ground‑truth class), and debiasing losses include the product‑of‑experts (PoE) loss L_poe = −y · log softmax(log p_m + log p_b) that combines the main model prediction p_m and bias model prediction p_b, as well as example reweighting L_reweight = −(1−β) y · log p_m and confidence regularization that smooths a teacher prediction by β; performing IMP or mask training with these debiasing losses (particularly PoE, and also example reweighting and confidence regularization) produces subnetworks with higher OOD accuracy than subnetworks obtained when pruning with the standard cross‑entropy loss, while typically keeping ID accuracy near the full model's level for sparsities up to ~70%.

metadata.narrative: The paper provides multi-loss evidence that integrating debiasing objectives during pruning improves OOD (H4), and reports the trade-offs between ID and OOD for different debiasing methods. The load-bearing uncertainty is that debiasing effectiveness depends on the bias-model construction and may degrade ID under some tasks (P4, P8). Concretely, the conclusion holds as a practical rule-of-thumb for the studied bias definitions, but its universal applicability requires validating the bias-model design and the tolerable ID/OOD trade-off on deployment-specific criteria.

nodes.title: Applying debiasing objectives during pruning promotes OOD robustness of subnetworks

nodes.content: Using out‑of‑distribution (OOD) training examples as part of the mask‑optimization process reveals an empirical upper bound on attainable robustness: when the OOD training sets (for example, HANS training examples combined with MNLI training examples for natural language inference) are included during mask training, subnetworks pruned from a fine‑tuned BERT at sparsities between about 20% and 70% attain very high OOD accuracy (e.g., nearly 100% accuracy on HANS in the reported experiments) while maintaining ID performance close to the dense model, and analogous strong reductions of the ID–OOD gap are observed on PAWS and FEVER‑Symmetric; these results show that there exist sparse BERT subnetworks that are nearly unbiased with respect to the specific MNLI/QQP/FEVER dataset biases when OOD examples are available for mask search.

metadata.narrative: Using OOD training signals to find masks and thereby empirically upper-bound achievable robustness is a well-executed and persuasive experimental strategy (H2). The principal limitation is that these are supervised upper bounds that require representative OOD examples (P9). Thus the conclusion that "sparse, nearly unbiased subnetworks exist" is strongly supported as an existence/upper-bound statement under OOD supervision, but it does not by itself imply such subnetworks are discoverable without any OOD signal.

nodes.title: Including OOD training examples in mask training can produce nearly unbiased sparse subnetworks

nodes.content: Starting mask training from an intermediate checkpoint of the full BERT fine‑tuning process, instead of from the pre‑trained weights or from the final fully fine‑tuned weights, substantially reduces total compute while yielding subnetworks whose mask‑training convergence curves and final ID/OOD performance closely match those obtained when starting from the fully fine‑tuned model; for example, for MNLI the experiments show that beginning mask training from a checkpoint after approximately 20,000 fine‑tuning steps (about 55% of the full fine‑tuning schedule used in these experiments) produces final accuracy and convergence speed comparable to starting from the end‑of‑fine‑tuning checkpoint.

metadata.narrative: The timing experiments with checkpoint sweeps and mask-training curves (H5) credibly show that starting mask training from an intermediate fine-tuning checkpoint can reduce compute while producing comparable masks in the studied tasks. The dominant residual risk is that the optimal checkpoint is task- and seed-dependent and currently requires per-task calibration (P10). Hence the refinement is practically useful but not yet an automated, universally applicable recipe.

nodes.title: Starting mask training from an intermediate fine‑tuning checkpoint reduces compute with little loss

nodes.content: For very high sparsity targets (e.g., 90% parameter removal from the Transformer layers), gradually increasing sparsity during mask training and using the soft mask initialization improves both average ID/OOD performance and training stability relative to initializing mask training directly at the high sparsity. Concretely, the soft initialization sets each real‑valued mask element to the absolute value of its corresponding weight and the gradual schedule used in the experiments increases sparsity from 70% to 90% (implementation uses a cubic schedule), and ablation studies comparing fixed‑90% initialization to gradual 70%→90% schedules show that the gradual schedule with soft initialization attains higher ID accuracy, higher OOD scores on HANS/PAWS/FEVER‑Symmetric, lower variance across random seeds, and requires less additional training to reach comparable performance.

metadata.narrative: Ablations (Table 5, Fig. 8) provide concrete evidence that gradual sparsity increase and soft initialization materially improve mask-training at very high sparsity (H6), reducing variance and improving mean accuracies. The remaining uncertainty (P11) is whether these precise schedule choices generalize beyond the experimental settings; nonetheless the ablation gives constructive, reproducible recommendations for practitioners working at extreme sparsity.

nodes.title: Gradual sparsity increase and soft mask initialization improve results at extreme sparsity

nodes.content: Extending the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis to robustness, the pre‑trained BERT-base-uncased contains sparse subnetworks (task‑agnostic masked structures) that can be trained in isolation: when these subnetworks are fine‑tuned in isolation using either the standard cross‑entropy loss or a debiasing objective such as the product‑of‑experts PoE loss, they can match or outperform the full dense BERT on both in‑distribution and out‑of‑distribution evaluations, which indicates that maskable structures inside the pre‑trained model are compatible with debiased learning.

metadata.narrative: The paper presents a credible empirical extension of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis into the robustness domain, showing rewound pre-trained subnetworks can be fine-tuned with debiasing to match or exceed dense-model OOD performance in the studied regimes. The main load-bearing weaknesses are sparsity- and task-dependence (P12) and sensitivity of mask-search/fine-tuning choices; thus the extension is an important empirical observation but should be framed as conditional on the studied settings rather than a general theorem.

nodes.title: Pre‑trained BERT contains LTH-style SRNets trainable with CE or PoE fine‑tuning

nodes.content: The existence of sparse and robust subnetworks is not limited to BERT‑base: in limited experiments on other pre‑trained language model backbones, namely RoBERTa‑base and BERT‑large, mask training with the PoE debiasing loss produces sparse subnetworks that retain ID performance while improving OOD robustness. For example, on RoBERTa‑base a 50% sparse subnetwork obtained by mask training with PoE achieves an increase of 6.84 percentage points on the HANS OOD accuracy compared to the full RoBERTa fine‑tuned with standard cross‑entropy, at a small MNLI (ID) drop of 1.74 points, and similar positive effects of gradual sparsity schedules are observed on larger models in the reported experiments.

metadata.narrative: Experiments on RoBERTa-base and BERT-large (Table 6) materially strengthen the claim that the sparsity-vs-robustness phenomena generalize beyond BERT-base (H7). Remaining weaknesses are limited backbone/treatment coverage and reproducibility risk due to delayed code release and potential sensitivity to implementation details (P13, P14). Consequently, the generalization claim is plausible for related Transformer encoders under similar mask-training+PoE pipelines, but broader claims to all PLM families or to other pruning methods require further replication.

nodes.title: SRNet phenomena also observed for RoBERTa‑base and BERT‑large in limited settings

nodes.content:
In all mask‑training and iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) experiments that search for sparse subnetworks, the selection of the reported masks or checkpoints is performed by choosing the checkpoint with the best in‑distribution (ID) development‑set performance (ID validation), and consequently the out‑of‑distribution (OOD) accuracies reported for those selected subnetworks are measured after selecting masks/checkpoints using only ID validation rather than any OOD validation.
      Fig. 2; Fig. 3

metadata.failure_mode: If checkpoint selection by ID dev systematically favors masks whose OOD performance is idiosyncratically high on the reported OOD splits, then the conclusion that "SRNets preserve ID while improving OOD robustness up to ~70% sparsity" would be weakened: the concrete OOD gains reported in Figs. 2–5 could shrink or disappear under an alternate, deployment-style selection (e.g., selecting masks only by training-time criteria or via a held-out ID metric without per-mask validation tuning). The mechanism is that ID-driven selection is an implicit hyperparameter sweep that leaks information about which sparsity/mask variants are ultimately reported; the scope of damage is quantitative (the cited OOD improvements could be smaller or not statistically significant) and could flip the interpretation from "SRNets improve OOD" to "some masks happen to improve OOD on the reported splits."
metadata.weakness_reason: The pipeline uses ID-dev-driven model/mask checkpoint selection (the paper states "we select the best checkpoints based on the ID dev performance" except in special OOD-using experiments). If mask checkpoints are chosen to maximize ID dev, this selection can produce optimistic or non-representative OOD numbers (e.g., by favoring models that happen to generalize better on the particular OOD splits used), so reported OOD gains may partly reflect selection bias rather than robust improvement that would hold under ID-only selection in deployment.

nodes.title: Checkpoint and mask selection is done by ID dev performance, not OOD validation

nodes.content:
The experimental results reported for sparse subnetworks are averaged over four random seeds and include standard‑deviation bands to indicate variability, and the OOD evaluation is performed on three task‑specific OOD datasets (HANS for NLI, PAWS variants for paraphrase identification, and FEVER‑Symmetric for fact verification) rather than on a broader suite of OOD benchmarks, which limits statistical confidence and the breadth of OOD generalization claims.
      Fig. 2; Table 5

metadata.failure_mode: If the small-sample variability is larger than reported (e.g., some seeds give much worse OOD or ID performance) or if other forms of dataset bias are considered, then the conclusion that SRNets "can retain ≳95% ID performance and produce measurable OOD gains up to 70% sparsity" would be substantially qualified: the numeric claims (≳95% retention, measured OOD gains) might only hold on average or on particular seeds/datasets, not reliably across runs or bias types. Mechanistically, seed-dependent optimization failures and dataset-specific effects would mean SRNets exist only under restricted random seeds / bias types; scope of damage: reduces the generality and quantitative strength of the conclusion.
metadata.weakness_reason: Averaging over 4 runs provides only modest power to bound variability, especially for high-variance regimes (mask training at high sparsity); some plots and Table 5 show substantial seed variance at large sparsities. The OOD datasets used are canonical but limited in scope and type of bias (lexical overlap, claim-only signal). Both limited seeds and narrow OOD coverage increase uncertainty about whether the reported ID retention (>95%) and OOD gains generalize across random seeds, dataset splits, and other bias types.

nodes.title: Reported results use four random seeds and a limited set of OOD datasets

nodes.content:
The mask‑training implementation and IMP variants used in the experiments employ specific hyperparameter choices that materially affect outcomes: mask training uses two initialization variants (a hard variant that sets the real‑valued mask entries for the smallest‑magnitude weights to zero and the others to a fixed α·φ value, and a soft variant that initializes each real‑valued mask entry to the absolute value of the corresponding weight), controls sparsity either by fixing to a target sparsity or by gradually increasing sparsity on a schedule, dynamically adjusts the binarization threshold φ at a specified frequency Δt_φ, and uses substantially longer training for high sparsity because good subnetworks at high sparsity require more optimization; the experiments report that soft initialization together with gradual sparsity increase is used for the 70%→90% schedule and leads to better high‑sparsity results.
      Eq. (5); Eq. (6)

metadata.failure_mode: If alternative reasonable hyperparameter choices, shorter training budgets, or different initialization are used and lead to failures to converge to high-quality masks, then the conclusion's practical reach narrows: SRNets would still exist but only under specialized training recipes and budgets, which undermines the claim of general practical applicability (the mechanism is sensitivity of mask optimization to initialization/schedule; scope of damage: narrows from "can be found" to "can be found but only with particular heavy tuning and compute").
metadata.weakness_reason: The ability to find SRNets appears to depend on method choices (hard vs soft init, schedule ranges, number of epochs). If success hinges on carefully tuned schedules and longer training that are not standardized, the practical claim "SRNets exist up to 70% sparsity" is conditional: different sensible hyperparameter settings or lower compute budgets could fail to find those subnetworks. This is an uncertain bridge because the paper documents some ablations but does not fully map the reachable region of hyperparameters where SRNets are reliably found.

nodes.title: Mask‑training/IMP use specific inits, schedules, thresholds and longer training for high sparsity

nodes.content:
The debiasing procedures evaluated (product‑of‑experts PoE, example reweighting, and confidence regularization) depend on a separately trained bias model that is trained on hand‑crafted spurious features designed for each task: for MNLI and QQP the bias model uses word‑overlap features (e.g., whether the hypothesis is a subsequence of the premise, the fraction of hypothesis words appearing in the premise, and similarity statistics computed from fastText vectors), and for FEVER the bias model uses max‑pooled claim embeddings computed from fastText word vectors; the bias model outputs a class probability vector p_b and the bias degree β for an example is defined as the bias model's predicted probability of the ground‑truth class, and β is then used to adjust the main training loss via PoE, example reweighting, or confidence regularization.
      Section 3.3; Appendix B.3.1 (bias feature definitions)

metadata.failure_mode: If the hand-crafted bias features poorly capture the spurious signals present in other datasets or in different types of bias, then applying the same PoE workflow during pruning or mask training would not produce the same OOD gains; the conclusion that SRNets "improve OOD robustness" would be limited to the particular bias definitions used in the paper (mechanism: debiasing optimization steers masks toward features defined by the bias model; scope: conclusion loses generality across bias types and depends on external bias-model choices).
metadata.weakness_reason: The measured bias degree β and hence the effectiveness of PoE-style debiasing depend on the chosen spurious features and the bias-model capacity. If the bias model does not capture the dominant spurious cues or if the spurious features are misspecified, the debiasing loss may misestimate example difficulty and either under- or over-correct for bias; consequently the observed OOD improvements for subnetworks obtained with PoE may be contingent on the specific bias-model design rather than indicating a general property of sparsity vs robustness.

nodes.title: Debiasing methods rely on a bias model trained on hand‑crafted spurious features

nodes.content:
The procedure used to obtain pre‑trained tickets follows a train–prune–rewind pipeline: iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) is applied during fine‑tuning to produce a pruning mask, and for the IMP variant with weight rewinding the subnetwork parameters are then rewound to the pre‑training parameter vector θ_pt (i.e., the pre‑trained weights) before fine‑tuning the masked subnetwork in isolation; these implementation and selection details of the rewinding pipeline affect whether the identified pre‑trained subnetworks fine‑tune to robust ID and OOD performance.
      Eq. (3)

metadata.failure_mode: If alternative rewinding choices (different rewind snapshot, different pruning fractions per iteration) produce masks that fail to fine-tune into robust solutions, then the conclusion "pre-trained BERT contains subnetworks that when identified prior to fine-tuning can match or exceed dense model ID/OOD" would be narrowed to "under specific rewinding and mask-search protocols these pre-trained tickets exist", reducing the generality of the claimed Lottery Ticket extension to robustness.
metadata.weakness_reason: The ability of rewound masks to fine-tune into robust solutions depends on which iterations are rewound to (pre-trained weights vs early fine-tuning checkpoints), how many pruning iterations and the rewind protocol. Small changes in the rewind point or in IMP hyperparameters can change whether the rewound subnetwork can recover ID accuracy or OOD generalization after isolated fine-tuning; the paper gives specific protocols but not a comprehensive sensitivity map.

nodes.title: IMP with weight rewinding and rewound‑mask fine‑tuning determine whether pre‑trained tickets fine‑tune robustly

nodes.content:
Applying mask training directly on the pre‑trained parameter vector θ_pt (i.e., learning masks while keeping pre‑trained weights frozen) produces subnetworks that are competitive with the dense baseline at sparsities at or below about 50%, but the experiments report degraded ID performance for subnetworks found from pre‑trained mask training compared to subnetworks derived from mask training initialized on fine‑tuned weights (the "bert‑pt subnet" exhibits worse ID performance than the "bert‑ft subnet" in the reported results).
      Fig. 4; Fig. 5

metadata.failure_mode: If, for many realistic sparsity budgets (e.g., >50%), pre-trained masks routinely fail to fine-tune to dense-model-level ID/OOD performance, then conclusion 2 would be false as stated for moderate-to-high sparsity: the extension of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis to OOD robustness would hold only in a narrower sparsity window rather than broadly up to ~70%.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim that pre-trained tickets fine-tuned in isolation can match or beat the dense model is sensitive to sparsity regime: the paper itself documents that pre-trained-mask subnetworks underperform in ID (and sometimes OOD) relative to masks searched on fine-tuned weights, especially beyond 50% sparsity. Thus the strongest version of conclusion 2 is contingent on sparsity and task; if the effect holds only at lower sparsities, the general claim "match or beat" must be scoped accordingly.

nodes.title: Mask training on pre‑trained weights is competitive up to 50% sparsity but often worse than starting from fine‑tuned weights

nodes.content:
Comparative evaluations across tasks and pruning scenarios show that mask training generally achieves better ID/OOD trade‑offs than iterative magnitude pruning at moderate sparsity levels, though there are task‑dependent exceptions—particularly at extreme sparsity (e.g., 90%) or on specific tasks where IMP can be competitive—so the relative benefit of mask training depends on mask initialization, sparsity regime, and the downstream task.
      Fig. 2; Fig. 3

metadata.failure_mode: If further tuning of IMP or different IMP schedules produce comparable results, then the claim that "mask training is generally more effective than IMP at moderate sparsity" becomes weaker: practitioners might find that either method can be preferable depending on hyperparameter tuning and task (mechanism: sensitivity to pruning schedule and retraining protocol); scope of damage: conclusion needs to be restated as "mask training often outperforms IMP under our hyperparameter choices and tasks" rather than a broad general rule.
metadata.weakness_reason: The empirical superiority of mask training over IMP is supported by plotted curves, but the effect size varies across tasks, sparsities, and initialization variants (hard vs soft). The conclusion risks over-generalization: mask training's advantage may hold in the studied setups (hyperparameters, datasets) but could be smaller or reversed under alternate budgets or model variants not exhaustively explored.

nodes.title: Mask training generally outperforms IMP at moderate sparsity with task‑dependent exceptions

nodes.content:
Pruning or mask training with debiasing objectives (PoE, example reweighting, confidence regularization) often produces subnetworks with higher OOD accuracy than pruning with standard cross‑entropy, while mostly preserving ID accuracy up to moderate sparsities, but the effectiveness depends on the bias‑model setup and task: some debiasing variants cause slight ID accuracy drops even as OOD improves, and confidence regularization in particular tends to preserve more ID performance at the cost of milder OOD gains.
      Fig. 2; Fig. 3; Fig. 9

metadata.failure_mode: If for certain realistic deployment constraints the ID drop induced by PoE-based pruning is unacceptable or if the bias model is misaligned with deployment bias, then the conclusion that "including debiasing objectives during pruning promotes OOD robustness while preserving ID up to ~70% sparsity" would need to be qualified: debiasing-in-pruning can help but may require task-specific tuning and explicit ID/OOD trade-off decisions (mechanism: loss reweighting changes optimization basins; scope: reduces immediacy of the prescription to "apply PoE during pruning").
metadata.weakness_reason: Debiasing-in-pruning uses the same bias-model machinery noted in P4; observed improvements are method- and task-dependent and sometimes come with ID degradation. The paper documents these trade-offs but does not fully quantify when ID loss outweighs OOD gains for downstream application constraints, making the practical claim contingent on user priorities and bias-model fidelity.

nodes.title: Debiasing‑in‑pruning effectiveness varies with bias model and can trade ID for OOD gains

nodes.content:
Experiments that include OOD training examples during mask training (for example, combining HANS training examples with MNLI training examples for mask search) produce subnetworks that can reach near‑perfect OOD performance (e.g., near‑100% accuracy on HANS at 20%–70% sparsity), thereby establishing an empirical upper bound on achievable robustness for those OOD test sets; however, these results depend critically on the availability and the representativeness of the OOD training data used during mask optimization.
      Fig. 6; Fig. 10

metadata.failure_mode: If available OOD examples are scarce, biased, or unrepresentative of realistic deployment OOD conditions, then the conclusion that "sparse, nearly unbiased subnetworks exist" as an upper bound is of limited practical value: the nearly-unbiased masks are achievable only with OOD supervision and do not imply that purely ID-driven searches will find comparably unbiased subnetworks (mechanism: optimization moves toward OOD patterns only when such supervision is present; scope: weakens the practical implication that SRNets could be found without OOD data).
metadata.weakness_reason: Achieving near-perfect OOD performance when OOD data is included is an empirical upper bound for the specific OOD datasets and added examples; however, such results rely on having representative OOD supervision. This does not demonstrate that the same robustness is discoverable without OOD signals (the paper acknowledges this as an open question) and the bound depends strongly on how representative and numerous the OOD examples are (e.g., FEVER-Symm2 had only 708 examples and required upsampling as noted in B.3.3).

nodes.title: Including OOD examples in mask training yields strong OOD gains but depends on OOD data availability/representativeness

nodes.content:
Mask training started from intermediate full‑BERT fine‑tuning checkpoints (for example, after roughly 20,000 MNLI fine‑tuning steps, which corresponds to about 55% of the full fine‑tuning schedule used in these experiments) attains final subnetworks whose performance is comparable to mask training started from the end‑of‑fine‑tuning checkpoint while reducing total compute; determining the optimal intermediate checkpoint to start mask training requires per‑task calibration and cannot be predicted universally from the reported curves.
      Fig. 7; Fig. 11

metadata.failure_mode: If the checkpoint that yields comparable masks varies substantially across tasks, seeds, or datasets and cannot be predicted cheaply, then the practical benefit (reduced compute while preserving mask quality) is fragile: practitioners may still need to train large dense models to near completion or perform expensive tuning to locate the right intermediate checkpoint, reducing the reported cost advantage (mechanism: sensitivity of mask-search to starting point; scope: narrows the practical claim to "can reduce compute if one can find the right checkpoint, which currently requires extra overhead").
metadata.weakness_reason: The claimed compute savings hold for the studied tasks and hyperparameter budgets, but the optimal checkpoint timing appears task- and seed-dependent; the authors note that predicting the exact timing is intractable without full curves and propose early-stopping heuristics as potential but unvalidated solutions. Thus practical deployment would need per-task calibration and might not realize the same savings uniformly.

nodes.title: Starting mask training from intermediate fine‑tuning checkpoints reduces compute but needs per‑task calibration

nodes.content:
For extreme target sparsities such as 90% the experimental protocol that gradually increases sparsity (e.g., from 70% to 90% using a cubic schedule) combined with the soft mask initialization (initializing each real‑valued mask entry to the absolute value of its corresponding weight) materially improves mask‑training outcomes: ablation studies comparing fixed‑90% hard initialization to gradual 70%→90% soft initialization show substantially higher ID and OOD accuracies and lower variance when using the gradual schedule with soft initialization.
      Table 5

metadata.failure_mode: If alternative datasets, seeds, or larger-scale models exhibit different dynamics such that gradual sparsity + soft init no longer stabilizes training at extreme sparsity, then the conclusion that gradual sparsity increases improve SRNets at very high sparsity would be weaker: the improvement would be an empirical recipe applicable in studied setups rather than a general method guaranteed to yield high-quality masks at 90% across settings (mechanism: varying optimization landscape at extreme sparsity; scope: reduces generality of the claim).
metadata.weakness_reason: The ablation table provides quantitative evidence that gradual schedules plus soft init improve performance and reduce variance at extreme sparsity. However, improvements are measured under the specific cubic schedule ranges and training epochs selected; it remains possible that alternative schedules or other details could further change outcomes, and stability at 90% is still limited (some seeds fail without gradual schedules), so the approach helps but is not a universal remedy.

nodes.title: Gradual sparsity schedules with soft init materially help extreme‑sparsity mask training

nodes.content:
The claim that pre‑trained BERT contains rewound subnetworks that can be fine‑tuned in isolation to match or outperform the full dense model on both ID and OOD evaluations holds in some sparsity regimes and under specific fine‑tuning objectives: empirical results show that subnetworks rewound to pre‑trained weights and then fine‑tuned with either standard cross‑entropy or PoE can match or exceed dense model performance in particular sparsity ranges, supporting an extension of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis to robustness that is nevertheless conditional on sparsity and fine‑tuning choices.
      Fig. 4

metadata.failure_mode: If for other tasks, model sizes, or bias types rewound tickets cannot be fine-tuned to robust solutions, then the conclusion that "pre-trained BERT contains SRNets trainable in isolation with debiasing or standard fine-tuning" would be overstated: the LTH extension to robustness would be an empirical observation limited to the studied regimes rather than a general hypothesis extension (mechanism: task- and sparsity-dependence; scope: narrows claim to studied settings).
metadata.weakness_reason: The reported extension is empirical and conditional: success is shown up to particular sparsities and depends on whether debiasing is used during fine-tuning. The LTH-type claim for robustness is therefore not a formal statement but an observed phenomenon in selected tasks and sparsity windows; the broader applicability to other tasks, models, or bias types is uncertain (the paper itself highlights limitations in Section 6 and open questions)."

nodes.title: Extension of Lottery Ticket to robustness depends on sparsity regime and debiasing during fine‑tuning

nodes.content:
Generalization experiments are limited to two additional pre‑trained model backbones: RoBERTa‑base and BERT‑large; in these limited settings the paper reports that mask training with the PoE debiasing loss on standard fine‑tuned checkpoints produces 50% sparse subnetworks that preserve ID performance while improving HANS OOD accuracy (evidence summarized in the reported model comparison table), but the scope of these evaluations is narrow relative to all possible backbone and task combinations.
      Table 6

metadata.failure_mode: If other model families (encoder-decoder, autoregressive) or other pruning methods do not exhibit the same sparsity-robustness patterns, then the conclusion that the phenomena generalize would need to be constrained to BERT-family encoders and the specific mask-training+PoE pipeline; scope of damage: reduces claim from broad "other PLMs" to "some larger BERT-family variants under similar treatment."
metadata.weakness_reason: The generalization claim is supported by experiments on two additional backbones but those are limited: only mask training with PoE is tested, and results are reported for NLI only (Table 6). Broader claims about "other PLM variants" require more architectures, tasks, and compression methods; the current evidence supports transfer to some related Transformer backbones but not a universal generalization.

nodes.title: Generality to other PLMs shown only for RoBERTa‑base and BERT‑large under limited settings

nodes.content:
Reproducibility is constrained by two implementation details: the authors indicate that code and reproduction scripts will be released upon publication (the paper marks the code release checklist item as not released at the time of writing), and all experiments were executed on single GPUs (Nvidia V100 and TITAN RTX) with training details documented in Appendix B, but the code, exact random seeds, and hyperparameter sweep scripts were not publicly available at the time the paper was written, which poses a reproducibility risk.
      Checklist; Appendix B.2

metadata.failure_mode: If replication attempts using the reported descriptions fail due to missing implementation details or hidden tuning, then the conclusion about generalization to other backbones would be less credible until independent reproduction is available; scope of damage: reduces community confidence and practical adoptability until code and exact recipes are shared.
metadata.weakness_reason: Reproducing complex mask-training schedules, gradual sparsity schedules, and specialized selection heuristics can be sensitive to implementation details. Without immediate code/data release, small differences in data preprocessing, bias-model construction, or mask-threshold scheduling could make the experiments hard to replicate, weakening confidence that the RoBERTa/BERT-large generalization will be reproducible in other groups' setups.

nodes.title: Reproducibility risk from withheld code and single‑GPU runs

nodes.content: The paper evaluates subnetworks across three pruning/fine-tuning paradigms (prune-after-finetune, prune-before-finetune with rewinding, mask-training without weight updates), multiple pruning algorithms (IMP, IMP with rewinding, mask training), and multiple debiasing objectives (PoE, example reweighting, confidence regularization), reporting ID/OOD outcomes for each combination on three NLU tasks.

metadata.credit: This comprehensive factorial coverage is a load-bearing strength for Conclusion 1: showing similar SRNet phenomena across pruning paradigms and debiasing objectives reduces the chance that the reported SRNets are an artifact of a single algorithm or training pipeline. It guards against a major alternative explanation (that SRNets only appear for one ad-hoc method) and thus substantively increases confidence that sparsity-vs-robustness coexistence is not a single-method fluke; the scope of support is experimental generality across the studied axes.

nodes.title: Consistent multi-paradigm experimental coverage (three pruning/fine-tuning paradigms, several debiasing losses)

nodes.content: The authors explicitly include OOD examples (HANS, PAWS training splits, and upsampled FEVER-Symm data) in mask training to measure an empirical upper bound on achievable OOD accuracy for subnetworks, demonstrating nearly 100% HANS accuracy for subnetworks pruned from fine-tuned BERT at 20–70% sparsity (Fig. 6 and Section 4.5).

metadata.credit: This direct OOD-supervised mask training is a strong, load-bearing strength for the claim that "sparse, almost unbiased subnetworks exist": it shows concretely that the optimization objective can find sparse masks that reach very high OOD accuracy when OOD signals are available, thereby providing an empirical ceiling that validates the expressivity of sparse masks and separates optimization or search limitations from representational impossibility. Without this experiment, evidence that sparsity alone suffices to achieve unbiasedness would be far weaker.

nodes.title: Using OOD training data to empirically bound achievable robustness

nodes.content: Comparative plots in Figs. 2–4 consistently show mask-training curves outperforming IMP in the moderate sparsity regime across NLI, paraphrase, and fact verification tasks, with detailed discussion in Sections 4.2.2 and 4.3.2 and cross-task consistency in Appendices.

metadata.credit: The repeated, cross-task empirical advantage of mask training over IMP provides a load-bearing comparative strength for Conclusion 3: it supports the practical recommendation that practitioners prefer mask optimization when aiming for SRNets at moderate sparsity. Because the advantage is observed across tasks and pruning scenarios, it rules out an explanation that mask training won on a single lucky dataset or seed and instead indicates a robust pattern within the studied regime.

nodes.title: Ablation evidence showing mask training advantage in multiple figures and tasks

nodes.content: Ablation experiments in Section C.1 and Fig. 9 show that pruning/mask training with different debiasing objectives (PoE, example reweighting, confidence regularization) almost consistently improves OOD performance compared to CE-based pruning while preserving acceptable ID performance.

metadata.credit: The fact that several independent debiasing objectives produce OOD gains when integrated into the pruning stage is a load-bearing strength for Conclusion 4: it indicates that the beneficial effect is not exclusive to a single loss construction but emerges across multiple bias-aware formulations, thereby increasing confidence that incorporating bias-aware objectives during pruning is a generally useful lever to improve subnetwork robustness rather than an idiosyncratic artifact of PoE alone.

nodes.title: Consistent improvements from multiple debiasing losses during pruning

nodes.content: Sections 5.1 and Figures 7 and 11 present mask-training curves starting from checkpoints at varied fine-tuning steps, showing that starting mask training from an intermediate checkpoint (e.g., 20k steps on MNLI) achieves convergence speed and final accuracy comparable to starting from the fully fine-tuned model.

metadata.credit: The explicit timing sweep and convergence plots are a load-bearing strength for Conclusion 6: they provide direct empirical evidence that an intermediate checkpoint suffices to recover mask quality, and therefore substantiate the practical compute-saving recommendation. This guards against the alternative that only complete fine-tuning yields viable masks and quantifies how much of fine-tuning can be skipped in the studied tasks.

nodes.title: Mask-training starting-point sweep and plotted convergence curves support the timing claim

nodes.content: Table 5 and Fig. 8 present ablations comparing fixed vs. gradual sparsity schedules and hard vs. soft mask initialization at 90% sparsity, showing that gradual schedules with soft init (e.g., 0.7→0.9) improve mean ID/OOD accuracy and reduce seed variance across datasets.

metadata.credit: The ablation evidence is a concrete, load-bearing strength for Conclusion 7: it demonstrates that the proposed gradual-sparsity + soft-init refinement materially improves mask-training success at extreme sparsity and reduces instability across seeds, thereby justifying the recommendation rather than leaving it as an anecdotal observation.

nodes.title: Ablation table and reduced-variance evidence for gradual sparsity schedules at extreme sparsity

nodes.content: Table 6 reports mask-training + PoE results on RoBERTa-base and BERT-large for MNLI/HANS, showing 50% sparse masks that preserve ID and improve HANS accuracy (e.g., +6.84 HANS for RoBERTa with a small MNLI drop), and similar trends for gradual schedules on larger models (Section C.5).

metadata.credit: Empirical success on two additional, substantially different PLM variants is a load-bearing strength for Conclusion 9: it indicates the sparsity-vs-robustness phenomena extend beyond BERT-base to other Transformer backbones and scales, which materially strengthens the claim that SRNets are not a BERT-base-only curiosity and supports practical adoption across related models.

nodes.title: Cross-backbone experiment confirming SRNet phenomena on RoBERTa-base and BERT-large

steps.reasoning: State the goal and define SRNets: a sparse and robust subnetwork (SRNet) is a subnetwork identified by applying a binary mask $\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pr}|}$ to the model's prunable parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pr}$ (the Transformer-layer and classifier weights) such that the masked model $f(\mathbf{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta})$ (where $\odot$ denotes the Hadamard product) substantially reduces prunable parameters (e.g., achieves sparsity $s$ up to 70%) while preserving in-distribution (ID) performance and improving or preserving out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness relative to the standard cross-entropy-fine-tuned dense model. This definition follows the paper's description of subnetworks and pruning goals.

Start from the upstream result (known): mask training often outperforms IMP at moderate sparsity in finding SRNets (the result established previously). Treat this as a given starting point for the broader empirical claim about SRNets' existence across paradigms and datasets.

Describe the comprehensive experimental scope used to test SRNet existence: experiments use the BERT-base-uncased backbone (about 110M total parameters, roughly 84M in Transformer layers, with sparsities reported relative to the 84M), three NLU tasks (MNLI/HANS for NLI, QQP/PAWS for paraphrase identification, FEVER/FEVER-Symmetric for fact verification), multiple pruning/fine-tuning paradigms illustrated in the paper (prune a fine-tuned BERT, prune pre-trained then fine-tune the subnetwork with rewinding, and mask-training-based pruning without parameter updates), two pruning methods (IMP and mask training), and both standard cross-entropy $\mathcal{L}_{\text{std}}$ and debiasing objectives such as product-of-experts $\mathcal{L}_{\text{poe}}$. Results are reported as ID and OOD metrics and averaged across runs.

Present empirical evidence from subnetworks pruned from CE fine-tuned BERT (prune-after-finetune paradigm): the paper reports that using any of the four pruning methods examined (IMP and mask training, each with CE and PoE variants), BERT can be compressed up to 70% sparsity while still preserving at least ~95% of the full model's ID performance; additionally, standard pruning sometimes yields small but measurable OOD improvement over the full BERT (HANS/PAWS/FEVER-Symmetric), and PoE-based pruning produces even larger OOD gains with only slight ID degradation remaining above the 95% threshold. These observations and quantitative curves are shown in the paper's figure summarizing subnetworks pruned from CE fine-tuned BERT. 
Fig. 2

Present empirical evidence from subnetworks pruned from PoE fine-tuned BERT: when the full BERT is fine-tuned with the product-of-experts debiasing objective prior to pruning, the resulting subnetworks maintain comparable ID and OOD performance up to 70% sparsity, demonstrating that SRNets can be found even when OOD generalization is explicitly optimized during full-model fine-tuning. This supports the redundancy of parameters even under debiasing objectives. 
Fig. 3

Present empirical evidence from subnetworks fine-tuned in isolation (prune-before-finetune / rewinding paradigm): the authors obtain masks from pre-trained BERT via either IMP with rewinding or mask training, rewind weights to pre-trained initializations, and then fine-tune the sparse subnetwork in isolation; results (reported in the figure for subnetworks fine-tuned in isolation) show that these pre-trained-ticket subnetworks can match or sometimes outperform the full dense model on ID and OOD evaluations at sparsity levels up to roughly 50–70% depending on the task, especially when mask-training-derived masks are used and when PoE is used during downstream fine-tuning. This demonstrates that SRNets can be identified before downstream adaptation and then trained in isolation to yield robust solutions. 
Fig. 4

Present empirical evidence from subnetworks obtained without any parameter fine-tuning (mask training on pre-trained BERT): applying mask training directly to the frozen pre-trained BERT and optimizing masks with CE or PoE losses yields subnetworks under 50% sparsity that are competitive with the CE- or PoE-fine-tuned full BERT on ID and OOD metrics; in some cases (e.g., on PAWS and on FEVER under 50% sparsity) the mask-trained subnetworks from pre-trained BERT match the performance of subnetworks found in the fine-tuned BERT. These results are shown in the corresponding figure. 
Fig. 5

Aggregate the empirical patterns across paradigms and tasks to reach the conclusion: combining the experimental findings (prune-after-finetune, prune-before-finetune with rewinding, and mask-only paradigms) and leveraging the upstream knowledge that mask training is effective at moderate sparsity, the paper demonstrates that BERT contains sparse and robust subnetworks (SRNets) up to approximately 70% sparsity that (a) retain at least about 95% of the full BERT's ID performance and (b) produce measurable OOD gains on HANS, PAWS, and FEVER-Symmetric relative to the standard cross-entropy fine-tuned dense model. The authors explicitly report these cross-dataset and cross-paradigm empirical regularities and present the supporting figures. 
Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5

Start from the upstream result (known): mask training is generally more effective than IMP at moderate sparsity for identifying SRNets. Treat that comparative effectiveness as an established empirical fact to be used when evaluating pre-trained-ticket behavior.

Define the pre-trained-ticket (rewind) pipeline used to find trainable subnetworks in pre-trained BERT: given the pre-trained parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pt}$, obtain a mask $\mathbf{m}$ either by iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding (IMP-rw) applied to a trained model and rewinding the remaining parameters to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pt}$, or by mask training that learns $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ from a (possibly fine-tuned) model and then extracting a binary $\mathbf{m}$; subsequently fine-tune the masked model $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{L}_1}(f(\mathbf{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pt}))$ on the downstream task. This is the train-prune-rewind approach adapted from the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis pipeline described in the paper.

Describe the experimental objective for tickets fine-tuned in isolation: maximize the sum of ID and OOD evaluation metrics of the fine-tuned masked model $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{L}_1}(f(\mathbf{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pt}))$ subject to a sparsity constraint $\frac{\|\mathbf{m}\|_0}{|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pr}|}=1-s$, where $\|\cdot\|_0$ is the $L_0$ norm and $|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pr}|$ is the number of prunable parameters. This formal objective mirrors the paper's optimization formulation for the pre-trained ticket case.

Present empirical evidence from experiments fine-tuning tickets in isolation: results plotted in the figure for BERT subnetworks fine-tuned in isolation show that (1) mask-training-derived subnetworks (found with PoE during mask training) and then fine-tuned in isolation often produce OOD performance superior to the full CE fine-tuned dense BERT, indicating reduced susceptibility to dataset bias; (2) under PoE-based fine-tuning, both IMP-derived and mask-training-derived subnetworks are generally comparable to the full BERT fine-tuned with PoE on ID and OOD; and (3) for most subnetworks, PoE fine-tuning ("poe ft") outperforms standard CE fine-tuning ("std ft") in OOD metrics, suggesting the importance of debiasing during fine-tuning even when the subnetwork structure contains less-biased solutions. These empirical observations are explicitly discussed in the paper's analysis of the relevant figure. 
Fig. 4

Interpretation tying to the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH): because the pre-trained BERT contains masks $\mathbf{m}$ that, when applied to the pre-trained weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pt}$ and then fine-tuned in isolation, recover ID performance and, in many cases, improve OOD robustness, the findings extend the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis to the robustness setting: there exist pre-trained "trainable tickets" inside BERT that are compatible with debiased learning and can match or beat the dense model on both ID and OOD evaluations. This extension is explicitly claimed by the authors based on the experimental results.

Define iterative magnitude pruning (IMP): IMP is a magnitude-based pruning algorithm that alternates between training the full model and pruning a fraction of parameters with smallest absolute values, then re-training the pruned subnetwork, and repeating until the target sparsity is reached; IMP as implemented uses per-step pruning ratio $\Delta s$, pruning interval $\Delta t$, and (for IMP with rewinding) returns the mask rewound to an earlier parameter state. This description follows the magnitude-based pruning formulation and the iterative procedure described in the paper's pruning methods. 
[19]

Define mask training: mask training treats a binary pruning mask $\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ as trainable by associating a real-valued mask $\hat{\mathbf{m}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ with frozen model weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, deriving $\mathbf{m}$ from $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ via binarization $\mathbf{m}_{i,j}=1$ if $\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{i,j}\geq\phi$ and $0$ otherwise, and applying the straight-through estimator to backpropagate gradients through the binarization to update $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$. Here $\phi$ is a threshold and $\mathcal{L}$ denotes the training loss. The forward binarization and straight-through gradient estimation procedure is explicitly used in the paper's mask training implementation. 
[3]

State the experimental comparison objective and setup: the authors compare IMP and mask training as pruning methods $p\in\{\text{imp},\text{mask}\}$ across multiple downstream tasks (natural language inference with MNLI/HANS, paraphrase identification with QQP/PAWS, fact verification with FEVER/Fever-Symmetric), across pruning/fine-tuning paradigms (prune-after-finetune, prune-before-finetune with rewinding, mask-training without updating weights), and using both standard cross-entropy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{std}}$ and debiasing losses (e.g., product-of-experts $\mathcal{L}_{\text{poe}}$). The evaluation metrics used are ID accuracy or F1 and OOD accuracy/F1 as appropriate; reported results are averaged over multiple runs and best checkpoints are selected based on ID dev performance unless otherwise specified.

Present the empirical evidence summarized from the pruning-from-fine-tuned-BERT experiments: when subnetworks are extracted from the CE fine-tuned BERT and evaluated across sparsity levels, the mask-training-based subnetworks generally yield better ID/OOD trade-offs than IMP at moderate sparsities (e.g., up to 70%), as shown by higher OOD accuracies (HANS/PAWS/FEVER-Symmetric) while preserving ID performance. This observation is described in the paper's discussion of the results and illustrated by the performance curves and error bands. 
Fig. 2

Record the specific exceptions and high-sparsity behavior observed in experiments: the paper reports that IMP can be competitive or sometimes better than mask training at very high sparsity (e.g., 90%) on certain tasks (for example, IMP outperforms mask training at 90% sparsity on the fact verification task in some settings), and that for particular combinations (e.g., "mask train (poe)" at 90% sparsity on QQP and FEVER) mask training may underperform. These task- and sparsity-dependent exceptions are explicitly noted by the authors when comparing IMP and mask training. 
Fig. 2

Present corroborating evidence from pruning-from-PoE-fine-tuned-BERT experiments: on subnetworks derived from a BERT fine-tuned with the product-of-experts debiasing loss, mask training still tends to outperform IMP at moderate sparsity, while IMP can match or surpass mask training at some extreme sparsities; the paper reports that PoE-based pruning yields similar comparative behavior between mask training and IMP, supporting the generality of the comparison across pruning objectives. 
Fig. 3

Synthesize the empirical conclusion: based on the definitions of IMP and mask training and the systematic empirical comparisons across datasets, pruning paradigms, sparsities, and training losses, conclude that mask training is generally more effective than IMP at identifying sparse and robust subnetworks (SRNets) at moderate sparsity levels, producing better ID/OOD trade-offs across tasks and pruning scenarios, while acknowledging that IMP can be competitive in certain high-sparsity corners of the experimental space.

Define the debiasing objectives used during pruning: a bias model produces bias-model predictions $\mathbf{p}_b=(\mathbf{p}_b^1,\dots,\mathbf{p}_b^K)$ and bias degree $\beta=\mathbf{p}_b^c$ for the ground-truth class $c$, which can be used to form debiasing losses such as the product-of-experts loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{poe}}=-\mathbf{y}\cdot\log\text{softmax}(\log\mathbf{p}_m+\log\mathbf{p}_b)$ where $\mathbf{p}_m$ is the main model prediction distribution and $\mathbf{y}$ is the one-hot ground-truth distribution; other debiasing losses include example reweighting $\mathcal{L}_{\text{reweight}}=-(1-\beta)\,\mathbf{y}\cdot\log\mathbf{p}_m$ and confidence regularization $\mathcal{L}_{\text{confreg}}=-\mathrm{S}(\mathbf{p}_t,\beta)\cdot\log\mathbf{p}_m$ with smoothing function $\mathrm{S}(\cdot)$ as defined in the paper. These loss definitions are those the authors use when integrating debiasing into pruning. 
Fig. 9

Explain the motivation for applying debiasing during pruning: standard pruning pipelines typically minimize the standard cross-entropy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{std}}$ on ID data and therefore may preferentially remove parameters unrelated to ID loss while leaving parameters that exploit dataset bias intact; thus, incorporating bias-aware objectives into the pruning stage could direct pruning to preserve parameters that contribute to unbiased solutions or to remove bias-exploiting parameters, potentially producing sparse subnetworks with improved OOD generalization. This reasoning is the conceptual motivation the authors articulate prior to the experiments.

Describe how debiasing objectives are applied in pruning methods: during IMP or mask training, the authors replace or augment the pruning/training loss $\mathcal{L}_2$ with $\mathcal{L}_{\text{poe}}$ or other debiasing objectives so that the mask optimization or magnitude-based pruning decisions are guided by bias-aware losses rather than standard CE alone; in mask training this means updating the real-valued masks $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ with gradients of the debiasing loss via the straight-through estimator, and in IMP this means using debiasing losses when re-training between pruning iterations.

Present empirical evidence that pruning with debiasing losses improves OOD: the paper reports that mask training or IMP performed with the PoE loss (and likewise with example reweighting or confidence regularization) yields subnetworks that have higher OOD accuracy than subnetworks obtained via CE-based pruning, while preserving strong ID performance up to roughly 70% sparsity; in particular, "mask train (poe)" and "imp (poe)" subnetworks show larger OOD gains in the prune-from-fine-tuned-BERT experiments, and mask-training-with-PoE on pre-trained BERT also yields competitive results. The authors explicitly discuss these comparisons and illustrate them in their figures. 
Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 9

Record the interpretive claim the authors draw from these observations: because debiasing-in-pruning produces subnetworks with improved OOD performance without sacrificing much ID accuracy, integrating debiasing objectives into pruning or mask training is a viable mechanism to obtain sparse models that are more robust to dataset bias; the authors further note that mask-training results showing robust subnetworks inside a CE-fine-tuned full model imply that biased full models may nonetheless contain sparse, less-biased solutions discoverable when pruning is bias-aware.

Define the "upper bound" experimental setup: include OOD training examples (training examples drawn from the out-of-distribution set, e.g., HANS for NLI) in the mask-training optimization so that the mask variables $\mathbf{m}$ (or real-valued masks $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$) are optimized with access to OOD signals; the goal is to empirically measure how unbiased and robust a sparse subnetwork can become when OOD supervision is available. This setup applies across the three pruning/fine-tuning paradigms formulated in the paper (the prune-from-fine-tuned model formulation maximizing ID+OOD evaluations under sparsity, the pre-trained-ticket formulation, and the mask-only formulation where parameters are frozen and only masks are learned).

State the datasets and evaluation used for the upper-bound experiment: for NLI the OOD dataset is HANS, for paraphrase identification OOD is PAWS (PAWS-qqp and PAWS-wiki), and for fact verification OOD is FEVER-Symmetric (v1 and v2); evaluation metrics are accuracy for NLI and FEVER and F1 for paraphrase identification. The OOD training examples are combined with ID training data when constructing the mask-training objective, and test evaluations use the respective standard OOD test sets.

Report the specific empirical findings on NLI (HANS) when using OOD information during mask training: subnetworks pruned from a fine-tuned BERT ("bert-ft subnet") at sparsities between 20% and 70% achieve nearly 100% accuracy on HANS while maintaining ID performance close to the full BERT; subnetworks obtained from the pre-trained BERT ("bert-pt subnet") also achieve very high OOD accuracy though with worse ID performance than the fine-tuned-subnetwork variant; subnetworks obtained by rewinding pre-trained masks and then fine-tuning ("bert-pt subnet + ft") attain the best ID performance but the poorest OOD performance among the three, yet still reach nearly 90% HANS accuracy at 50% sparsity. These observations are explicitly reported in the paper's analysis of Figure 6. 
Fig. 6

Report corroborating empirical findings on paraphrase identification and fact verification: mask training that includes OOD examples substantially narrows the ID–OOD performance gap on PAWS and FEVER-Symmetric; although the subnetworks do not always reach 100% OOD accuracy as on HANS, they nonetheless attain large reductions in bias-induced errors and significantly improved OOD metrics compared to the full dense model, as shown in the additional plots. The paper notes an exception on Symm2 (FEVER-Symmetric variant) where the OOD upper bound appears limited, likely due to the small size of available OOD data (708 examples), which suggests data-quantity sensitivity in estimating the upper bound. 
Fig. 10

Synthesize the conclusion about the empirical upper bound: by directly incorporating OOD training data into mask training across the three pruning/fine-tuning paradigms, the experiments reveal that there exist sparse subnetworks (at sparsities between 20% and 70% relative to Transformer-layer parameters) that are nearly unbiased with respect to the MNLI training-set bias (e.g., achieving nearly 100% HANS accuracy) while keeping ID performance close to that of the dense model; similar substantial OOD gains and narrowed ID–OOD gaps are observed on PAWS and FEVER-Symmetric, establishing an empirical upper bound on obtainable robustness when OOD signals are available during mask optimization.
Start from the upstream result (known): mask training is an effective method to find SRNets at moderate sparsity; use this as context for exploring practical compute-reduction strategies.

Define the computational cost problem and the proposed mitigation: fully fine-tuning the dense PLM before searching for subnetworks is computationally expensive; the authors propose starting mask training from an intermediate fine-tuning checkpoint $f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)=\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{L}_{std}}^t(f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{pt}))$ (i.e., after $t$ steps of CE fine-tuning) instead of waiting for full convergence, thereby reducing total compute while potentially preserving subnetwork quality. The mask training procedure thereafter optimizes mask variables $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ with the selected thresholding schedule.

Describe the experimental procedure used to evaluate timing: the authors perform mask training on checkpoints taken at different fine-tuning steps $t$ (including $t=0$ pre-trained, intermediate steps such as $t=20{,}000$, and the "ft to end" fully fine-tuned checkpoint), and plot mask-training curves showing validation accuracy versus mask-training optimization steps for these different starting checkpoints; the experiments focus on representative sparsity levels (e.g., 70% for MNLI) and report convergence speed and final accuracy. 
Fig. 7

Report the empirical findings for MNLI: the mask-training curve that starts from the pre-trained checkpoint ($t=0$) converges slower and to a worse final accuracy on HANS compared with the mask-training curve that starts from the end-of-fine-tuning checkpoint; however, starting mask training from a checkpoint obtained after approximately $20{,}000$ fine-tuning steps (which is roughly 55% of full fine-tuning steps used in the experiments) yields mask-training curves whose convergence speed and final accuracy are competitive with starting from the fully fine-tuned checkpoint. This observation is explicitly described in the paper's figure and text. 
Fig. 7

Report corroborating findings for other tasks and note practical percentages: mask training for paraphrase identification (QQP) can start from about $15{,}000$ fine-tuning steps (≈44% of full training) and for FEVER from about $10{,}000$ steps (≈44% of full training) to achieve competitive mask-training performance relative to starting from the fully fine-tuned checkpoint; these numbers and curves are reported in the appendix figures summarizing the mask-training behavior across datasets. 
Fig. 11

Acknowledge limitations and practical considerations: the authors note that accurately predicting the single optimal checkpoint to start mask training (i.e., the minimal $t$ that guarantees comparable subnetwork OOD/ID performance) is difficult without observing the full set of mask-training curves, and they suggest that early-stopping heuristics might be a practical approach while leaving precise automatic prediction as future work. This qualification appears in the paper's discussion.

Synthesize the conclusion about practical refinement: based on the experimental evidence that mask training started from an intermediate fine-tuning checkpoint (e.g., ≈20{,}000 steps for MNLI) yields mask-training curves and final subnetwork performance comparable to starting from the fully fine-tuned model while reducing the total required compute of the full-model fine-tuning stage, conclude that starting mask training from an intermediate checkpoint substantially reduces compute while producing competitively performing subnetworks.

Start from the upstream result (known): mask training is an effective method to find SRNets at moderate sparsity, but the authors observe sharp performance drops when directly training at extreme sparsities (e.g., 90%). Treat this observation as background motivating schedule modifications.
