State the optimization difficulty at extreme sparsity and the proposed remedy: initializing mask training directly at very high target sparsity (e.g., 90%) drastically reduces model capacity at the outset and commonly causes optimization failure or severe performance degradation; to mitigate this, the authors propose gradually increasing sparsity during mask training (e.g., a cubic schedule increasing sparsity from 70% to 90%) and adopting the soft mask-initialization variant (where the real-valued mask initialization uses the absolute values of weights $\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{i,j}=\mathrm{abs}(\mathbf{W}_{i,j})$) to ease optimization. The hard and soft initialization variants are defined in the paper.

Describe the experimental comparison between fixed-sparsity and gradual-sparsity strategies: the authors run mask-training experiments at target 90% sparsity and compare (a) fixed initialization to 90% using the hard and soft mask initializations versus (b) gradual sparsity increase schedules such as 0.7→0.9, 0.5→0.9, and 0.2→0.9 while using the soft initialization for gradual schemes; evaluations include ID and OOD metrics across MNLI/HANS, QQP/PAWS, and FEVER/Symm datasets and include multiple random seeds to assess variance. 
Fig. 8

Report quantitative ablation results: Table 5 (the ablation table) shows that gradual sparsity-increase schedules (particularly 0.7→0.9) combined with the soft mask initialization produce higher ID and OOD accuracies and lower variance than fixed-sparsity initializations across most datasets; for example, on MNLI/HANS the 0.7→0.9 schedule yields better final accuracies than fixed initialization, and similar improvements are seen on QQP/PAWS and FEVER/Symm, with the 0.7→0.9 schedule achieving the best results on 7 out of 8 datasets in the ablation. These numerical comparisons are explicitly reported in the paper's ablation table. 
Table 5

Synthesize the conclusion about high-sparsity training: based on the optimization rationale and the empirical ablations showing higher accuracies, lower variance, and reduced required training when using gradual sparsity increases and soft initialization, conclude that gradually increasing sparsity during mask training (e.g., cubic schedule from 70% to 90%) and using the soft mask initialization substantially improves ID/OOD performance and stability at very high sparsity compared to training directly at fixed high sparsity.

Start from the upstream result (known): pre-trained BERT contains subnetworks that can be rewound and fine-tuned in isolation to match or beat the dense model on ID/OOD (conclusion 2 established earlier). Treat that as a given.

Define the extension target: extend the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) claim by evaluating whether the pre-trained BERT contains subnetworks that are trainable in isolation and that, after fine-tuning with either standard cross-entropy $\mathcal{L}_{\text{std}}$ or debiasing objectives such as product-of-experts $\mathcal{L}_{\text{poe}}$, can match or outperform the full dense model on both ID and OOD metrics. This extends the LTH notion from pure ID recoverability to OOD robustness.

Summarize the empirical evidence supporting the extension: in experiments where masks are learned from pre-trained or fine-tuned checkpoints (via IMP with rewinding or via mask training) and then the resulting sparse models are fine-tuned in isolation with either CE or PoE loss, the paper reports that (a) mask-training-derived and IMP-rewound tickets fine-tuned with PoE often outperform the dense CE model on OOD while matching ID, and (b) under PoE fine-tuning the tickets are generally comparable to the full PoE-fine-tuned model, demonstrating that the pre-trained masked structures encode solutions compatible with debiased learning. These outcomes are illustrated in the figure reporting subnetworks fine-tuned in isolation. 
Fig. 4

State the claimed conceptual generalization: based on the empirical results showing that pre-trained masked structures can be fine-tuned with debiasing or standard objectives to produce robust task solutions, assert that the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis extends to the robustness context: task-agnostic masked structures inside the pre-trained model encode solutions that are compatible with debiased learning and can be trained in isolation to yield robust models. This claim is explicitly made by the authors following their experimental section.

Start from the upstream result (known): there exist sparse and robust subnetworks inside BERT up to ~70% sparsity that preserve ID performance and improve OOD robustness (conclusion 1). Treat that empirical phenomenon as established for BERT-base and use it as the basis for testing generalization to other PLM variants.

State the generalization hypothesis and experimental procedure: test whether the primary sparsity-versus-robustness phenomena observed for BERT-base extend to other pre-trained Transformer variants and scales by conducting mask training with PoE loss on standard fine-tuned RoBERTa-base and BERT-large backbones, and evaluating ID (MNLI) and OOD (HANS) performance across sparsities (e.g., 50% and 70%), including experiments with gradual sparsity schedules where applicable.

Report the RoBERTa-base quantitative result: Table 6 reports that for RoBERTa-base, a 50% sparse mask-trained subnetwork (mask training with PoE on the standard fine-tuned RoBERTa backbone) attains HANS accuracy higher by 6.84 points compared to the full RoBERTa trained with standard CE ("full model std") while incurring a small MNLI (ID) drop of 1.74 points; this explicit numeric comparison demonstrates that SRNets with improved OOD robustness exist in RoBERTa-base. 
Table 6

Report the BERT-large quantitative and qualitative results: Table 6 and the accompanying discussion show that BERT-large exhibits the same qualitative phenomena: mask training with PoE can find 50% sparse subnetworks that preserve ID performance and improve or match OOD performance, and gradual sparsity increase schedules are effective for larger models as well; the authors also note that vanilla mask training can exhibit higher variance at 70% sparsity on BERT-large but that gradual schedules reduce variance and improve reliability. 
Table 6

Conclude the generalization claim: from these cross-backbone experiments and the reported numeric improvements (e.g., the 6.84-point HANS gain on RoBERTa-base at 50% sparsity with only a 1.74-point MNLI drop), conclude that the primary sparsity–robustness phenomena reported for BERT-base generalize to other PLM variants such as RoBERTa-base and BERT-large, supporting broader applicability of the SRNets findings.

open_questions.content: The authors explicitly acknowledge and identify several scientific issues left unresolved by this work: (1) Generalization beyond BERT-like NLU settings: this study focuses on BERT-family encoders and three NLU tasks; it remains open whether SRNets with similar ID/OOD trade-offs exist across other model families (e.g., encoder-decoder or autoregressive PLMs such as T5 or GPT), other tasks (generation, dialogue, multimodal), and other forms of dataset bias (e.g., demographic biases in dialogue or generation). (2) Predicting the optimal timing to start mask training to minimize total compute: while mask training starting from intermediate fine-tuning checkpoints can reduce cost, accurately and automatically predicting the minimal fine-tuning point (the checkpoint that yields subnetworks comparable to starting from full fine-tuning) remains unresolved; devising practical early-stopping or checkpoint-selection criteria that guarantee minimal compute without degrading subnetwork OOD performance is left for future work. (3) Robust subnetwork search at extreme sparsity and stability: although gradual sparsity increase and soft mask initialization improve results at very high sparsity (e.g., 90%), reliably finding high-quality, low-variance SRNets at extreme parameter budgets is still challenging; methods that further improve optimization stability and final OOD/ID trade-offs in this regime are an open direction. (4) Discovery of unbiased subnetworks without access to OOD data: this work uses OOD examples to estimate an upper bound on achievable unbiasedness; whether comparable almost-unbiased subnetworks can be identified using only ID data plus bias models (i.e., without any OOD supervision) is not resolved and remains a practical open problem.
